newsitem.title: USA: Analysts lukewarm on Reynolds changes.
newsitem.headline: Analysts lukewarm on Reynolds changes.

text.p: Analysts gave a lukewarm welcome to the much anticipated organizational changes announced by Reynolds Metals, and were still waiting to see what becomes of the company's lucrative packaging division.
"While they (Reynolds) think they are making great progress, I still think that the Street feels there has not been enough implementation to date," Clarence Morrison of Prudential Securities said.
Reynolds was just formalizing what, to a great extent, was already in place, and left in the air the issue of spinning off packaging, Morrison added.
The company is being officially reorganized into six worldwide, market focused businesses, effective April 1. The new set up will make it easier for any packaging spin off, Reynolds said.
Packaging had sales of $800 million in 1995, Prudential said.
"From my standpoint it was long on reorganization but a little short on restructuring. I expected something more definitive," Morrison said.
Reynolds said in a statement Thursday, "Reynolds continues to anticipate announcing the details of its Portfolio Review in the second quarter."
Analysts noted that unlike some of the other new business units, the global packaging and consumer products division will report to Reynolds chairman and chief executive officer, Jeremiah Sheehan.
"It gives me a little more confidence in the fact that the evaluation continues on the possibility of spinning that out as a separate unit," analyst Dan Roling of Merrill Lynch said.
There has been talk in the industry for some time that Reynolds would exit certain plants, with parts of recycling and rolling suggested by some.
"I think they would like to announce they are closing some plants, but they cannot do this because they have to notify labor," one analyst commented.
Having fewer business units and clearer lines of responsibility should improve results ultimately, Roling said.
Merrill Lynch expected Reynolds to earn 5-10 cents a share in the first quarter, while Prudential forecast 10 cents and maintained its Buy recommendation.
Reynolds lost 13 cents a share in the fourth quarter of 1996. Losses would have been worse if the company had not raised $9 million or 14 cents a share from liquidating inventories.
Savings of $100 million have been identified and further liquidation of inventory should also cushion the company's bottom line this year.
Reynolds agreed to sell its El Campo, TX extrusion plant to Tredegar Industries earlier this month for an undisclosed sum as part of a review of all its plants and businesses.
